title: The dawn verse
hookLine: the verse that wakes Rama on his first morning away from home is still sung at dawn
carry: pray at sandhya, where night meets day

lines: A HYMN AT DAWN IN SOUTH INDIA.
ITS FIRST VERSE IS FROM THE RAMAYANA.
cards: In many homes and temples in South India, the day starts with a recording of a Sanskrit hymn, the Venkatesha Suprabhatam, a song to wake the Lord at Tirupati. Its very first verse isn't new.
It's borrowed, word for word, from the Ramayana: what Vishvamitra says to wake Rama on his first morning away from home, sleeping on grass by a river. But first, the boys have to leave.

teach.b: Vasishtha, the royal priest, speaks to the frightened king. You've given your word, he says. Breaking it would undo all your merit.

And Vishvamitra knows every divine weapon there is; Rama will be safer with him than anywhere. Dasharatha yields, and keeps his word. He calls for Rama, and Lakshmana, who won't be left behind, and blesses them.
The boys walk out after the sage, bows in hand, and the text says a soft breeze blew and flowers fell from the sky.

teach.h: BALA AND ATIBALA BY THE RIVER.
teach.b: On the south bank of the Sarayu, Vishvamitra teaches Rama two mantras, bala and atibala, strength and great strength: with these, he says, you won't feel hunger or thirst or tiredness.
That night the princes sleep on grass, like ordinary travelers.

teach.h: A SAGE WAKES THEM AT DAWN.
teach.b: At dawn the sage wakes them: kausalya supraja rama purva sandhya pravartate, uttishtha narashardula kartavyam daivam ahnikam. Rama, fortunate son of Kausalya, the dawn twilight is here.
Rise, tiger among men; the day's sacred duties are waiting. The boys rise, bathe and say their prayers before they walk on.
Listen to the word in the middle of that verse: sandhya, the meeting point of night and day.

teach.h: KAUSALYĀ SUPRAJĀ RĀMA PŪRVĀ SANDHYĀ PRAVARTATE.
teach.b: Hindus have long treated these junctions, dawn and dusk above all, as times to turn to God; the daily prayer at them is called sandhya-vandana, honoring the twilight. That's why the verse still works.
Every morning at Tirupati, the temple wakes the Lord with the words a sage used to wake a prince, and many homes wake with him.

how: The Venkatesha Suprabhatam, sung at dawn at the Tirumala temple and played in many homes, opens with Vishvamitra's verse from the Bala Kanda waking Rama.

o: great strength, a mantra Vishvamitra teaches Rama
the dawn verse the sage uses to wake the boys
a heavy bow given to Rama as he leaves home

p: tells the king to keep his word
where night meets day: a time to pray

s: Dasharatha changes his mind because Rama insists
it's Vasishtha's counsel that persuades him to keep his word.
the first verse of the Venkatesha Suprabhatam comes from the Ramayana
it's Vishvamitra waking Rama on the road.
for Hindus, dawn is just the start of the workday
dawn and dusk are sandhya, junctions of the day kept for prayer; the boys pray before they walk on.

games.q: you're Rama, waking on grass on your first morning from home. the sage says the dawn twilight is here. what comes first?
o: start walking; there's a sacrifice to guard.
bathe and say your prayers at sandhya.
sleep a little longer; it's been a long day.
games.why: the boys rise, bathe and pray before they walk on. the verse that woke them now wakes the Lord at Tirupati each dawn.

practice: Try what the boys did at sandhya: before the phone, before the news, turn first toward the sacred. Sit facing the light if you can. Breathe in: the night is done.
Breathe out: the day's duties are waiting, and they can wait one more breath. If you pray, say one line to God, a name, a verse, the start of the Suprabhatam if you know it.
If you don't, simply greet the day before it starts asking things of you.

wordCard.voice: Atibala, great strength, one of the two mantras Vishvamitra teaches Rama on the road, before he wakes him with the dawn verse.

orig.note: Sanskrit atibalā: great strength. with balā, strength, the two mantras Vishvamitra teaches Rama.

carryVoice: Your line: pray at sandhya, where night meets day. A sage woke a prince with a verse, and temples still do. Day four hundred ninety-nine, done.

sources.q: kausalyā suprajā rāma pūrvā sandhyā pravartate

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda 21–22 (Vasishtha's counsel; departure; bala and atibala)
